study.title: Deuteronomy 15 Remission, generosity and consecration to the Lord
study.overview: Deuteronomy 15 organizes three areas of the life of God's people under the covenant: the cancellation of debts in the seventh year, generous care for the poor brother and the liberation of the Hebrew servant, in addition to the consecration of the first animals to the Lord. The chapter shows that obedience to God was not just ritual: it reached economics, social justice, work and worship. The rule of remission was not a license for exploitation, but a brake on oppression and a call to rely on the divine provision. At the same time, the text insists that poverty should not harden the heart of the rich; the hand should remain open. Finally, holiness also appears on the table: the people could eat the offering, but without treating blood as food, for life belongs to God.

outline.title: Remission of debts and promise of provision
outline.explanation: Every seven years there was remission: debts among brothers should be released, while the collection of the foreigner remained. The aim was to avoid the perpetuation of misery within the covenant community. The text connects this practice to God's blessing on earth, showing that generosity depends on trust in his word and obedience to his commandments.

outline.title: Hand open to the poor, without hardness of heart
outline.explanation: If there were a needy among the brethren, the people should not close their hearts or their hand. The closeness of the year of remission could not become an excuse to deny help. The commandment treats inner thinking as a serious moral matter: refusing help by avarice is sin, and the abundance received by God must flow for the benefit of the needy.

outline.title: Liberation of the Hebrew Servant with dignified provision
outline.explanation: The Hebrew servant or the serva Hebrew should be freed in the seventh year of service. The exit should not be empty; you had to provide resources taken away from the blessing received. If the servant desired to remain for love of the home and the well received, there was a rite of permanence. The text also recalls Egypt to support the dignity of the liberated and the benevolence of the lord.

outline.title: Consecrated firstborn and blood shed
outline.explanation: The first males of the flock were to be sanctified to the Lord. If there was defect, the animal was not fit for sacrifice, but could be eaten in the villages, by clean and unclean people, as a common food. The only explicit prohibition is blood: it must not be eaten, but poured on the earth, a sign of reverence to the life given by God.

study.context: The notes provided place the chapter in the framework of the law of the year of remission, associated with the seventh year, and relate this principle to the liberation of servants and to the care of the poor. They also indicate that the legislation sought to prevent economic exploitation and preserve the survival of the needy within the people. There are no secure additional data on location, date or specific historical circumstances other than this legal framework.
study.theology: The chapter unites social justice and holiness. The remission of debts teaches that property and credit are not absolute before God; the covenant requires mercy, limits to the exploitation and memory of grace received. The insistence on giving up the poor shows that poverty is no reason for indifference, but an occasion to imitate divine generosity. The deliverance of the servant, accompanied by concrete provision, states that the freedom granted by God must be reflected in human relations without humiliation. The memory of Egypt bases ethics: who has been rescued cannot treat the other hard. Finally, the prohibition of eating blood states that life belongs to the Lord; worship also involves recognizing limits before divine holiness. Together, the chapter presents a people called to live as a community of grace, where worship, economy and compassion do not separate.

scholarViews.insight: The annual remission was a release of people in financial subjection, so that the poor would not be exploited and could survive deprivation.
The order to give up to the poor brother should not be annulled by the awareness that they would always need; this requires practical liberality and not indifference.
The blood of the animal represents his life, so consuming it would be to treat in a profane way something that belongs in a special way to God.

questions: How does my way of using resources - money, time, and influence - reflects the hand opening that God requires here?
In what situations can I be using caution as an excuse not to help someone who really needs it?
How should the memory of God's liberation shape the way it treats people under my responsibility?
study.practice: Practise this week a concrete generosity and measure: identify someone in real need and help without waiting for return, with discretion and dignity. Also review your attitudes toward debts, favors and commitments: where there is hardness, ask God for a more free and compassionate heart. As you read the chapter, remember that biblical holiness reaches both worship and the use of money and power.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not detail the exact scope of the remission in verse 2 beyond describing it as annual release; therefore, it is not appropriate to say more than that. There is also no basis in the notes to identify with historical precision the institutional scenario of Israel beyond the legal text itself. The interpretation presented follows a Protestant evangelical reading, but certain applications - especially about contemporary social and economic practice - are prudential inferences, not explicit statements of the chapter.
